general.name: General EP Fit Assessment
general.description: Critical thinking and emotional intelligence — measured two ways (forced-choice trait comparison and situational judgment) — the baseline test for every applicant.

items.text: Of these four, which is MOST like you, and which is LEAST like you?

options.text: I like having a backup plan ready before I need it.
When something goes wrong, I want to understand why before I fix it.
I usually notice when someone around me is upset, even if they don't say so.
I can hear criticism without feeling like I need to defend myself right away.

items.text: Of these four, which is MOST like you, and which is LEAST like you?

options.text: I can stay level-headed even when someone is being difficult with me.
Before I act on a report from someone else, I like to confirm it myself if I can.
When several things need attention at once, I deal with the most urgent one first.
I choose my words carefully when a conversation feels sensitive.

items.text: Of these four, which is MOST like you, and which is LEAST like you?

options.text: I'd rather find the real cause of a problem than just patch the symptom.
I take correction well, even when I don't love hearing it.
I can tell the difference between what's urgent and what just feels urgent.
I'd rather double-check something than assume it's accurate.

items.text: Of these four, which is MOST like you, and which is LEAST like you?

options.text: I can tell when someone's mood has changed before they mention it.
I know how to raise a difficult topic without making it worse.
My mood doesn't shift much even when I'm provoked.
I think through what could go wrong before I commit to a plan.

items.text: Of these four, which is MOST like you, and which is LEAST like you?

options.text: I can deliver an uncomfortable message without being harsh about it.
I keep my composure even when a situation gets tense.
I pick up on how people are feeling, even when it's subtle.
I focus on what matters most, even if something else feels more pressing.

items.text: Of these four, which is MOST like you, and which is LEAST like you?

options.text: I ask why something happened before I decide what to do about it.
I prepare an alternate option even when the main plan looks solid.
When something looks slightly off, I check it before moving forward.
Feedback doesn't put me on the defensive, even when it stings a little.

items.text: Attention check — please select "Agree" for this statement to show you're reading each item.
You're clearing a hotel room before your principal arrives. You find the door already unlocked, though housekeeping isn't scheduled. What's your best first move?

options.text: Treat it as a possible compromise: pause, notify your team lead, and re-clear the room with heightened caution before principal arrival.
Call the principal and delay their arrival until you're sure.
Lock the door yourself and continue as planned without telling anyone.
Assume housekeeping forgot to lock it and proceed with the sweep.

items.text: During a foot escort through a crowded venue, you notice the same person appears in your peripheral vision three times in different locations, each time looking away when you glance over. What do you do?

options.text: Make a mental note and continue as normal.
Quietly flag the pattern to your team via radio, adjust your position to put a barrier between the individual and principal, and keep monitoring.
Move closer to your principal and increase visual scanning without radioing the team.
Confront the person directly to ask why they're following you.

items.text: Your principal insists on taking a route you assessed as higher-risk because it's faster and they're running late. What's the right response?

options.text: Take the faster route without any additional precautions.
Silently comply and take the faster route without voicing the risk.
State the specific risk concisely, offer the safer alternative with the time difference, and defer to the principal's decision while adjusting your posture if they insist.
Refuse to proceed until they agree to the safer route.

items.text: You receive a radio report of "package moving" from a teammate, but you don't recognize the voice and the phrasing is slightly off from your team's standard code. What do you do?

options.text: Act on the report but stay alert for further confirmation.
Broadcast the exact same phrase back to confirm, over the same unsecured channel.
Ignore the report since it sounds unfamiliar.
Verify identity through a pre-established challenge/response or secondary channel before acting on the report.

items.text: Mid-shift, you realize you forgot to complete a pre-shift equipment check. What's the best move?

options.text: Complete the check immediately at the first safe opportunity and inform your supervisor of the gap.
Complete the check at the next scheduled break without telling anyone.
Skip it since the shift is already underway and nothing has gone wrong so far.
Wait until end of shift to check everything at once.

items.text: A principal snaps at you angrily over a scheduling mix-up that wasn't your fault. What's the best response in the moment?

options.text: Explain calmly that it wasn't your fault.
Stay calm, acknowledge their frustration without arguing fault, and focus on resolving the immediate issue.
Apologize even though it wasn't your fault, to de-escalate quickly.
Match their tone and defend yourself firmly.

items.text: You notice a teammate has been unusually quiet and short-tempered for the past two shifts. What do you do?

options.text: Call them out in front of the team for their attitude.
Mention it to your supervisor so they can address it.
Check in privately, ask if everything's okay, without pressing if they don't want to talk.
Say nothing, assuming it will pass.

items.text: A member of the public becomes visibly upset and raises their voice near your principal, though they pose no physical threat. What's the best approach?

options.text: Firmly tell them to leave the area immediately.
Physically block them without speaking to de-escalate first.
Wait to see if they calm down on their own before doing anything.
Calmly and respectfully create distance and redirect them while remaining non-confrontational.

items.text: You made a mistake that a client noticed and pointed out in front of others. How do you respond?

options.text: Acknowledge it briefly and professionally, without over-apologizing or getting defensive, and correct it.
Apologize repeatedly and appear visibly embarrassed.
Say nothing and just fix it silently.
Explain why it wasn't really your fault.

items.text: A new team member seems nervous and is asking a lot of questions during a briefing. What's the best reaction?

options.text: Answer but suggest they save questions for after the briefing.
Answer patiently and encourage the questions — better they ask now than assume later.
Give short answers to move the briefing along faster.
Show visible irritation at the questions.

estate.name: Estate Security Scenarios
estate.description: Five situational judgment scenarios specific to residential/estate protection.

items.text: A delivery arrives at the estate gate that wasn't on today's expected list. What do you do?

options.text: Wave them through since deliveries happen often.
Ask the driver who sent them and let them in if the answer sounds reasonable.
Verify the delivery against the household's scheduling system before allowing entry, and hold the driver at the gate until confirmed.
Allow entry but escort the driver directly and closely monitor them.

items.text: You notice a perimeter camera has been offline for six hours and no one reported it. What's your first move?

options.text: Report it and wait for maintenance to fix it before doing anything else.
Assume it's a minor glitch since nothing else seems unusual.
Note it in the log for the next shift to review.
Report it immediately, physically inspect that section of perimeter, and increase patrol frequency there until it's restored.

items.text: A household staff member you don't recognize asks you to let them into a normally restricted wing, saying the principal approved it verbally. What do you do?

options.text: Politely decline until you can verify the approval directly with the principal or through the standard access process.
Let them in without question since they seem to know the property.
Let them in and mention it to your supervisor afterward.
Let them in but stay with them the entire time.

items.text: A landscaping crew is scheduled to work near a ground-floor window with a clear sightline into the principal's office. What's the right call?

options.text: Ask the principal to close the blinds instead of adjusting your posture.
Confirm the crew's identity and schedule in advance, and station a visual on that area while they're working.
Let them work as scheduled without extra attention.
Cancel the landscaping without discussing it with anyone.

items.text: You're doing a nightly perimeter check and find a side gate unlocked that should always be secured. No signs of forced entry. What's your next step?

options.text: Leave it, assuming it was intentional since there's no damage.
Assume someone forgot and lock it without further follow-up.
Secure the gate immediately, then investigate who had access and when, and report the finding.
Secure the gate and mention it at shift change.

event.name: Event Security Scenarios
event.description: Five situational judgment scenarios specific to venue and crowd-based protection.

items.text: During a red-carpet arrival, a photographer pushes past the rope line to get closer to your principal. What's the right response?

options.text: Firmly grab their arm and pull them back.
Ignore it since photographers often push boundaries.
Verbally warn them but don't physically reposition.
Calmly and firmly reposition between the photographer and principal, redirecting them back behind the line without escalating physically.

items.text: You're assigned to a single exit point at a crowded event and it becomes blocked by a growing crowd. What do you do?

options.text: Immediately communicate the blockage to the team and identify or prepare an alternate egress route for the principal.
Wait to see if the crowd thins out naturally.
Do nothing since it's not your exit to manage.
Try to clear the crowd yourself before reporting it.

items.text: A guest with an all-access credential is acting erratically near the stage area. What's the best approach?

options.text: Publicly confront them in front of other guests.
Discreetly monitor and reposition closer, alert the team, without confronting them based on credential status alone.
Immediately revoke their credential and remove them.
Ignore it since they have proper credentials.

items.text: Weather turns severe mid-event and the venue hasn't announced a plan. What's your move?

options.text: Wait for venue staff to make an announcement before acting.
Continue as normal since the event organizers haven't said anything.
Proactively check with venue management for their severe weather protocol and prepare a principal evacuation route regardless of their answer.
Suggest to your principal that they might want to leave.

items.text: You're one of three agents covering an event and one agent doesn't check in at the scheduled radio time. What do you do?

options.text: Assume they're just busy and continue your post.
Wait until the next scheduled check-in to see if they respond then.
Leave your post to go look for them without notifying anyone.
Attempt to reach them immediately through multiple channels and escalate to the team lead if there's no response within a short window.

driving.name: Driving Security Scenarios
driving.description: Five situational judgment scenarios specific to transport and motorcade protection.

items.text: You're driving your principal and notice the same vehicle has been behind you through three consecutive turns that don't match a direct route. What do you do?

options.text: Execute a pre-planned surveillance detection route to confirm before taking evasive action, and notify your team.
Speed up dramatically to lose them without informing anyone.
Keep driving the planned route and hope it's coincidental.
Immediately take evasive driving maneuvers without confirming first.

items.text: Your planned route is suddenly closed due to construction with no warning. What's your best move?

options.text: Stop the vehicle to figure out a new route.
Switch to a pre-planned alternate route immediately and notify the team of the change.
Improvise a new route on the spot without any prior planning.
Continue trying to find a way through the closure.

items.text: While stopped at a red light, a pedestrian approaches the vehicle and knocks on the window. What do you do?

options.text: Roll down the window slightly to ask what they want.
Get out of the vehicle to address them directly.
Stay alert, keep doors locked, assess the situation, and be prepared to move if the light changes or things escalate.
Ignore them completely and stare forward.

items.text: You arrive at the destination and the expected parking/drop-off spot is occupied by another vehicle. What's your move?

options.text: Drop the principal in the middle of the street.
Circle the block until the spot opens up.
Park illegally nearby and hope for the best.
Use your pre-planned secondary drop-off point rather than improvising on the spot.

items.text: Mid-route, your principal asks you to make an unscheduled stop at a location you haven't assessed. What do you do?

options.text: Acknowledge the request, quickly assess the location's basic safety as you approach, and adjust your positioning accordingly.
Refuse the stop outright without explanation.
Comply without any additional assessment.
Try to talk the principal out of the stop.
